title: Weeknight Beef Bibimbap with Sesame Vegetables & Fried Egg
dek: Savory gochujang beef, warm rice, crisp cucumber, carrots, sprouts, seaweed and a fried egg become a colorful Korean-inspired dinner built for mixing.
image_alt: Beef bibimbap bowl with rice, a fried egg, carrots, cucumber, bean sprouts, seaweed and black sesame seeds
ingredients: 3 cups hot cooked short-grain white rice
8 oz mung bean sprouts, rinsed and drained
2 medium carrots, peeled and cut into matchsticks
1 cup prepared wakame seaweed salad, well drained
4 large eggs, preferably pasteurized if serving with soft yolks
2 tsp warm water, plus more as needed
2 tsp toasted black or white sesame seeds

instructions.name: Mix the clean sauces first
instructions.text: In one small bowl, stir 1 tablespoon soy sauce, brown sugar, 1 teaspoon sesame oil, half the garlic and all the ginger. In a second bowl, whisk the gochujang, 1 tablespoon rice vinegar, honey and warm water until spoonable. Keep both bowls away from the raw beef so the gochujang sauce stays ready for serving.

instructions.name: Season the crisp cucumber
instructions.text: Toss the cucumber with 1 teaspoon rice vinegar and 1/4 teaspoon kosher salt. Let it stand for 10 minutes, then drain away the released liquid. This quick seasoning keeps the slices crisp and prevents their moisture from pooling in the finished bowls.

instructions.name: Cook the sprouts and carrots separately
instructions.text: Heat a large 12-inch skillet over medium-high. Add 1/2 teaspoon neutral oil and the bean sprouts; cook for 2 minutes, then add 1 teaspoon soy sauce and cook 1 minute more. Transfer to a clean plate. Add another 1/2 teaspoon oil and the carrots, then cook for 3 to 4 minutes until flexible but still bright. Season with the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt and transfer beside the sprouts.

instructions.name: Brown and glaze the beef
instructions.text: Add 2 teaspoons neutral oil to the hot skillet. Crumble in the ground beef and press it into a broad layer. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes, then break it into bite-size pieces and continue cooking for 3 to 4 minutes. Drain excess fat if needed, stir in the soy-sugar mixture and cook for 1 to 2 minutes until glossy. Check several pieces with an instant-read thermometer and confirm the beef reaches 160°F. Transfer it to a clean bowl.

instructions.name: Fry the eggs to suit your diners
instructions.text: Wipe out loose browned bits and return the skillet to medium heat with the remaining 1 teaspoon neutral oil. Crack in the eggs, season lightly and fry for 3 to 4 minutes until the whites are fully set. For soft yolks, use pasteurized eggs; otherwise cover the skillet and cook until both whites and yolks are firm or the centers reach 160°F.

instructions.name: Build four colorful bowls
instructions.text: Divide the hot rice among four wide bowls. Arrange the glazed beef, bean sprouts, carrots, drained cucumber and drained wakame in distinct sections so each component remains visible. Set one fried egg in the center of every bowl, then add the scallions and sesame seeds.

instructions.name: Sauce, mix and serve
instructions.text: Spoon the gochujang sauce over the bowls or pass it at the table for adjustable heat. Encourage diners to break the yolk and mix the rice, beef, vegetables and sauce thoroughly before eating. Serve promptly while the rice and beef are hot and the cucumber remains cool and crisp.

why_it_works: Cooking sprouts and carrots in short separate batches removes excess moisture while preserving their individual color and texture, which is central to a well-defined bibimbap bowl.
Pressing the ground beef into a wide hot skillet creates browned surfaces before crumbling; the clean soy-sugar mixture then glazes the cooked meat without exposing a table sauce to raw beef.
Draining the seasoned cucumber and prepared seaweed prevents watery rice, while their cool crunch balances the hot beef, rice and egg.
A thinned gochujang sauce distributes evenly when the bowl is mixed, and serving it separately lets each diner control the fermented chile heat.
swaps: Replace ground beef with 12 ounces crumbled extra-firm tofu. Brown it in 1 additional tablespoon neutral oil, then glaze it with the same soy-sugar mixture.
Use baby spinach instead of prepared wakame. Wilt 6 ounces in the skillet for 1 to 2 minutes, squeeze away excess liquid and season with a few drops of sesame oil.
Brown rice works in place of short-grain white rice; cook it fully and serve it hot, allowing about 1/2 cup cooked rice per bowl.
For a mild bowl, replace half the gochujang with mild white or yellow miso and add warm water until the sauce is easy to drizzle.
storage: For best texture, store the rice, beef, cooked vegetables, cucumber, seaweed, eggs and sauce in separate airtight containers. Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 3 days. Reheat the rice, beef and cooked vegetables with a splash of water until they reach 165°F; add the cold cucumber, seaweed and sauce afterward. Fry fresh eggs when possible. Freeze the glazed beef for up to 2 months, but do not freeze the assembled bowls, cucumber or eggs.
notes: Prepared wakame salad is usually seasoned and can be salty. Drain it well, taste it before assembly and avoid adding extra salt to that component.
Use a 12-inch skillet and keep the vegetable batches separate. Crowding all the vegetables together steams them and blurs the crisp, individually seasoned textures.
Ground beef color is not a reliable doneness test. Measure 160°F in several pieces with a clean instant-read thermometer.
The calorie and cost estimates include the rice, beef, egg, vegetables, wakame and sauce. Prices vary most for prepared seaweed salad and gochujang.

faqs.q: Can I make bibimbap components ahead for weeknight dinners?
faqs.a: Yes. Cook the rice, beef, sprouts and carrots up to 3 days ahead, cool them promptly and refrigerate each component separately. Slice and season the cucumber on the day you serve it, then fry fresh eggs while the hot components reheat to 165°F.

faqs.q: How spicy is the gochujang sauce?
faqs.a: Two tablespoons make a medium sauce, but brands vary. Start each bowl with 1 teaspoon sauce and add more after mixing. For less heat, replace half the gochujang with mild miso; for more heat, serve extra gochujang at the table.

faqs.q: Why did my bibimbap turn watery after mixing?
faqs.a: The cucumber, sprouts or seaweed likely carried too much moisture. Drain the salted cucumber, cook the sprouts until their surface moisture evaporates and press excess dressing from the wakame. Use hot, freshly fluffed rice rather than wet or overcooked rice.
